parole.significato: -ous; -ose; -y; -ly Used to form adjectives from nouns.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian -usu, from Latin -ōsus.
Borrowed from Sicilian aicula (alongside àcula), from Latin aquila.
Borrowed from Sicilian anchi, from Latin hanc (“this”) + an uncertain word; see Italian anche for more.
Borrowed from Sicilian àngilu, àncilu, from Latin angelus (“angel”).
Borrowed from Sicilian apòstulu, from Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos).
Borrowed from Sicilian ària, metathesis of an earlier àira, from Latin āēr, from Ancient Greek ᾱ̓ήρ (āḗr). Doublet of ajru
Borrowed from Sicilian raloggiu, from Latin hōrologium, borrowed from Ancient Greek ὡρολόγιον (hōrológion), from ὥρα (hṓra) + λέγω (légō) + -ιον (-ion).
Borrowed from Sicilian artaru, from Latin altare.
Borrowed from Sicilian azzaru, from Latin aciarium, from acies.
Borrowed from Sicilian bastuni, eventually derived from Latin bastum. Compare Italian bastone, French bâton.
Borrowed from Sicilian patiri, from Vulgar Latin *patīre, from Latin patī. An early borrowing, as attested by the initial b-; compare biċċa.
Borrowed from Sicilian vasciu.
Early borrowing (with b- for p-) from Sicilian picciuni, from Latin pīpiōnem, of onomatopoeic origin.

Borrowed from Sicilian boccia, from Vulgar Latin *buttia, borrowed from Byzantine Greek βούττια (boúttia, plural of βούττιον (boúttion)), from Ancient Greek βοῦττις (boûttis), possibly borrowed from Pre-Greek.
Borrowed from Sicilian butiru, from Latin būtȳrum, from Ancient Greek βούτῡρον (boútūron).
Borrowed from Sicilian bisognu, from Vulgar Latin *bisonium, borrowed from Frankish *bisunnija.
Borrowed from Sicilian difisa, from Latin defensa.
Borrowed from Sicilian [Term?], from Late Latin dum interim.
Borrowed from Sicilian draguni, from Latin dracō.

parole.significato: pain, (chiefly) profound pain, emotional pain, suffering, sorrow
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian duluri, from Latin dolor.
Borrowed from Sicilian dutturi, from Latin doctor.
Borrowed from Sicilian fidari, from Vulgar Latin *fīdāre, from Latin fīdere. Unrelated to native feda (“to redeem”).
Integrated loan verb from Sicilian affugari, affucari, from Latin offocare. Cognate to English suffocate.

Borrowed from Sicilian falcuni, from Latin falcō (“falcon”), of Germanic origin, probably via Frankish *falko (“falcon, hawk”), from Proto-Germanic *falkô (“falcon”), from Proto-Indo-European *pol̑- (“pale”), from *pel- (“fallow”).
Borrowed from Sicilian fasola, from Latin phaseolus, from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos).
Borrowed from Sicilian fidi, from Latin fidem.
Borrowed from Sicilian ciuri (once fiuri), from Latin flōs. The singular in -a and the collective are backformations from the plural.
Borrowed from Sicilian forsi, from Latin forsit. Compare Italian forse.
Sicilian fràscinu, from Latin fraxinus.
Borrowed from Sicilian furchetta, diminutive of furca, from Latin furca.
Borrowed from Sicilian furnaru, from Latin furnārius.

Probably from Sicilian fusu, from Latin fusus (“spindle”); but perhaps merged with Arabic فُؤُوس (fuʔūs), plural of فَأْس (faʔs, literally “axe”), which is used figuratively for different kinds of protrusions (or is it conceivable that this Arabic use is itself influenced by the Latin?). The plural
Borrowed from Sicilian gaggia, from Latin cavea.
Borrowed from Sicilian gricali, from Latin graecalis, from graecus, thus “the direction of Greece”.
Borrowed from Sicilian mpurtari, from Latin importare.

Borrowed from Sicilian lignami (“wood”), from Early Medieval Latin lignāmen, derived from Latin lignum. The initial l- was reinterpreted as the Sicilian and/or Maltese definite article. Compare Italian legname.
Borrowed from Sicilian inspiegabbili, from Latin inexplicabilis.

parole.significato: to freeze; to turn in to ice
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian nghiazzari, derived from ghiazzu, ghiacciu (“ice”), from Latin glacies. Compare Tunisian Arabic [script needed] (galleṣ)

Borrowed from Sicilian littra, from Latin littera. The initial l- was interpreted as the definite article (Maltese l- and/or Sicilian l’) and hence deleted. Compare the opposite development in ilma, lemin, etc.

parole.significato: chalice, goblet (any large drinking vessel with a stem)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian càlici, from Latin calix.
From Sicilian càmmara, càmmira, ultimately from Latin camera from Ancient Greek καμάρα (kamára). Doublet of kamera and ċimnija.

parole.significato: chain (series of interconnected rings or links)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian catina, from Latin catēna. Cognate with English chain.

parole.significato: to throw out, expel, chase off
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian cacciari (“to chase, hunt”), from Latin captiare, captare, derived from capere. The fact that the first syllable has undergone imala speaks in favour of an early borrowing. Cognate to English capture
Borrowed from Sicilian cocu, from Latin coquus.
Borrowed from Sicilian cucca, ultimately from Latin cuculus ~ cucus. Hence doublet of kukù.
Borrowed from Sicilian corla, metathesis of còlira (“rage”), from Latin cholera, from Ancient Greek χολέρα (kholéra, “gastrointestinal disease”). For the sense compare choleric.
Borrowed from Sicilian coscia (“thigh”), from Late Latin coxa (“thigh”), from Proto-Italic *koksā, from Proto-Indo-European *kóḱseh₂, from *koḱs- (“joint, limb”) + *-eh₂.

parole.significato: a parent in-law, i.e. related by way of marriage
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian cugnatu, from Latin cognatus.
Borrowed from Sicilian cugnomi, from Latin cognomen. The similarity with Arabic كُنْية (kunya, “teknonym, byname”) is coincidental.
Borrowed from Sicilian cunsigliu, from Latin consilium.
Borrowed from Sicilian cuntentu, from Latin contentus.
Borrowed from Sicilian cuntestu, from Latin contextus.
Borrowed from Sicilian cuntrattu, from Latin contractus.
Borrowed from Sicilian cunventu, from Latin conventus.
Borrowed from Sicilian curuna, from Latin corona, from Ancient Greek κορώνη (korṓnē).
Borrowed from Sicilian cutra, probably eventually from Latin culcita, culcitra. Compare Italian coltre.

parole.significato: conscience (inner sense of morality; the attitude to one’s actions that it creates)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian cuscienza, from Latin conscientia.
From a diminutive of Sicilian cucciara, cucchiara, from Latin cochlearium, ultimately from Ancient Greek κοχλῐ́ᾱς (kokhlĭ́ās, “snail”).
From an augmentative of Sicilian cucciara, cucchiara, from Latin cochlearium.
Borrowed from Sicilian cucina, from Late Latin cocīna.
Borrowed from Sicilian lagu, from Latin lacus.
Borrowed from Sicilian àmitu (with a fused definite article), from Latin amidum, from older amylum, from Ancient Greek ἄμυλον (ámulon).
Borrowed from Sicilian isca (with fused definite article), from Latin esca.
Borrowed from Sicilian ligi, older variant of liggi, from Latin lex.
Borrowed from Sicilian liuni, from Latin leō, from Ancient Greek λέων (léōn).
Borrowed from Sicilian locu, from Latin locus.
Borrowed from Sicilian lucanda, from Latin locanda.
Borrowed from Sicilian livanti, from Latin levans.
Borrowed from Sicilian majistrali, from Latin magistralis.

Probably from underlying *mal-ajr (“with the air”), the latter word being a variant of arja that goes back to Sicilian airu (alongside aira, aria), from Latin aer (“air”). Aquilina’s suggestion to derive it from Arabic مُلامِل (mulāmil, “quick, swift”, of a mount) seems less likely.
From Sicilian mannara (“axe, large knife”), from Latin manuārius. Compare Italian mannaia.
Borrowed from Sicilian manzu.

parole.significato: mountain (large mass of earth and rock)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian muntagna, from Early Medieval Latin montānia, a collective based on Latin montem.

Borrowed from Sicilian muntuni, from Latin moltō, from Gaulish *multon-, from Proto-Celtic *moltos (“wether”). The plural mtaten instead of expected *mnaten seems to imply that the singular was formerly (also) pronounced *muttun.
Native derivation from the root, which is from Sicilian nnamurari, itself derived from Latin amor. Compare Italian innamorare, French enamourer.
Borrowed from Sicilian niputi, from Latin nepōs.
Borrowed from Sicilian pajisi, from Late Latin pāgēnsis.
Borrowed from Sicilian pariri, from Latin pareō (“to seem”).
Borrowed from Sicilian parrinu, from Early Medieval Latin patrīnus.
Borrowed from Sicilian patri, from Latin pater.
Borrowed from Sicilian pacienza, from Latin patientia.
Borrowed from Sicilian paci, from Latin pax.
Integrated loan verb from Sicilian pìnciri, from Latin pingere. Doublet of pitter, which compare.
Borrowed from Sicilian pitturi, from Latin pictor.
Borrowed from Sicilian pittura, from Latin pictura.

parole.significato: weight (quality of being more or less heavy)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian pisu, from Latin pensum.
Borrowed from Sicilian ponti, from Latin pons.

parole.significato: people (a group of persons forming or belonging to a particular nation)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian pòpulu, from Latin populus (“people”).
Borrowed from Sicilian portu, from Latin portus.
Borrowed from Sicilian punenti, from Latin ponens.

Singularised plural of qalza (“pant leg”), from older Sicilian *calza (“hose, stocking”), from Early Medieval Latin calcea, from Latin calceus (“shoe”). Compare contemporary Sicilian causi, cansi (“trousers”) and, with the original sense and form preserved, Italian calza (“sock, stocking”).
Borrowed from Sicilian campana, from Late Latin campāna.

parole.significato: A savoury pastry or dumpling, typically filled with ricotta cheese.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian cassata, originally probably “made with cheese”, from Vulgar Latin cāseāta, from Latin cāseus. Regarding the initial q- and the plural in -at probably a rather early borrowing.
Borrowed from Sicilian curti, corti, from Latin cohors.
Borrowed from Sicilian rizzettu, from Latin receptus. Compare Italian ricetto (“hut, shelter”). Doublet of riċetta.
Borrowed from Sicilian rìganu, from Latin origanum.
Borrowed from Sicilian rota, from Latin rota.
From older Sicilian *rucchellu (now ruccheddu), from a diminutive of Latin rocca (“distaff”), itself from Proto-Germanic *rukkô.
Borrowed from Sicilian urgiata, ultimately from Latin hordeum.

parole.significato: to rise from the dead, to be resurrected, resuscitated
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian risuscitari, from Latin resuscitare.

Borrowed from Sicilian saccu (“sack”), from Latin saccus, from Ancient Greek σάκκος (sákkos), from a language of the Ancient Near East. The Maltese sense from the use of straw-filled sacks as mattresses.
Borrowed from Sicilian savucu, from Latin sambūcus.
From Sicilian sirvituri, from Latin servitor.
Borrowed from Sicilian signali, from Latin signale.
Borrowed from Sicilian signuri, from Latin senior.

parole.significato: school (an institution dedicated to teaching and learning)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian scola, from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ).
Borrowed from Sicilian scorpiuni, from Latin scorpiō, from Ancient Greek σκορπίος (skorpíos).
Borrowed from Sicilian scuru, from Latin obscurus.
Borrowed from Sicilian solitu, from Latin solitus.
Borrowed from Sicilian nzunza, from Latin axungia.
Borrowed from Sicilian soru, from Latin soror. Cognate with English sister.
Borrowed from Sicilian spìritu, from Latin spiritus.
Borrowed from Sicilian spissu (“often”, literally “thickly”), from Latin spissus.
Borrowed from Sicilian splusioni, from Latin explosio.
Borrowed from Sicilian siccari, from Latin siccare.
Borrowed from Sicilian sucutari, variant of sicutari, from Vulgar Latin *sequitare, from Latin sequi.
Borrowed from Sicilian staggiuni, from Latin statio. Doublet of stazzjon (“station”).
Borrowed from Sicilian stidda, stilla, from Latin stēlla.
Borrowed from Sicilian timuni, from Latin temo. The word was also borrowed independently into Arabic as دُومان (dūmān).
Borrowed from Sicilian traduzzioni, from Latin trāductiō, trāductiōnem.

Borrowed from Sicilian tramuntana (“north wind; north”), from Latin transmontanus (“beyond the mountains”). The use for a north wind is found in several Romance languages; it seems not quite clear what mountains it originally referred to.

Borrowed from Sicilian pitrusinu, from Latin petroselinum, from Ancient Greek πετροσέλῑνον (petrosélīnon). Probably an early borrowing in which the initial pi- was interpreted as the preposition bi (“with”), thus Maltese bit-tursin (“with parsley”), whence the backformation. Compare, for more, this
Borrowed from Sicilian unuri, from Latin honor.
Borrowed from Sicilian valiggia, from Latin valisia.

parole.significato: a ship driven by a motor (of any kind)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Sicilian vapuri (“steam; steamship”), from Latin vapor.
Borrowed from Sicilian vuci, from Latin vōx.
Borrowed from Sicilian scupa, from Latin scopa.
Borrowed from Sicilian ciumara /sciumara (“river”), now limited to Calabria, ultimately from Latin flūmen.
Borrowed from Sicilian sciorta, sorta, from Latin sors. Doublet of xorti (“fate, luck”). In contemporary Sicilian the form with sci- seems less common, but it is still found.
Borrowed from Sicilian sciorti, sorti, from Latin sors. Doublet of xorta, which see.
Borrowed from Sicilian sciuttu, asciuttu, from Latin exsuctus.
Borrowed from Sicilian [Term?], from Vulgar Latin *salsa.
Borrowed from Sicilian zia, from Latin thia, from Ancient Greek θεία (theía).

Borrowed from Sicilian ziu, from Latin thius, from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos). Displaced the native Arabic terms għamm (“paternal uncle”) and ħal (“maternal uncle”), in part probably because this distinction is less relevant in the European family system.
Borrowed from Sicilian zimmiteru (variant of cimiteriu), from Latin coemeterium. Doublet of ċimiterju.
Borrowed from Sicilian chiaru, ciaru, from Latin clarus.

Borrowed from Sicilian ciattu, from Vulgar Latin *plattus, borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, “wide; broad”), from Proto-Hellenic *plətús, from Proto-Indo-European *pléth₂us, from *pleth₂- + *-us. Doublet of platt and piazza.
Borrowed from Sicilian ciavetta, from a diminutive of Latin clavis. Cognate to Italian chiavetta.
Borrowed from Sicilian cima.
Borrowed from Sicilian cimiteriu (variant of cimiteru), from Latin coemeterium. Doublet of zuntier.
Borrowed from Sicilian cinga, from Latin cingula, cingulum.
Borrowed from Sicilian cirasa, from Vulgar Latin ceresia.

Diminutive of older ċikken, still found in placenames. Probably from a now lost variant of Sicilian picculu, of uncertain origin, but with related forms throughout Romance. To the Maltese form compare especially Corsican cicculu, further also Spanish chico and pequeño, Italian piccolo and piccino, a
Borrowed from Sicilian circhettu, diminutive of circu (“circle, ring”), from Latin circus, from Ancient Greek κίρκος (kírkos).
Borrowed from Sicilian agghiandra, ghiànnara, ultimately from Latin glans, probably through the diminutive glandula.
Borrowed from Sicilian giugnu, from Latin iūnius.
Borrowed from Sicilian siguru, from Latin securus.
